cards.claim: The JEE (Advanced) 2026 syllabus lists elastic and inelastic collisions (with impulse and centre of mass) as a Mechanics topic. This entry does not name a projectile rebounding from a surface with energy loss, so the extension is covered only under the general collisions heading, not named in the syllabus.
cards.quote: Systems of particles; Centre of mass and its motion; Impulse; Elastic and inelastic collisions.

cards.claim: In an elastic collision the final kinetic energy equals the initial kinetic energy (the deformation is fully recovered without energy loss).
cards.quote: If the ‘spring’ connecting the two masses regains its original shape without loss in energy , then the initial kinetic energy is equal to the final kinetic energy but the kinetic energy during the collision time ∆t is not constant. Such a collision is called an elastic collision.

cards.claim: In an inelastic collision the deformation is only partly relieved and some of the initial kinetic energy is lost; this is the more common case.
cards.quote: The intermediate case where the deformation is partly relieved and some of the initial kinetic energy is lost is more common and is appropriately called an inelastic collision.

cards.claim: After an elastic rebound from a surface the particle still has its incoming speed, and the rest of the motion is an ordinary projectile problem (for example, projection up an incline).
cards.quote: (Hint: (i) After rebound, particle still has speed oV to start. (ii) Work out angle particle speed has with horizontal after it rebounds. (iii) Rest is similar to if particle is projected up the incline.)

cards.claim: Kinetic energy conservation fails in an inelastic collision, even after the collision is over, while linear momentum is still conserved.
cards.quote: (c) Linear momentum is conserved during an inelastic collision, kinetic energy is, of course, not conserved even after the collision is over.

cards.claim: Worked method from NCERT Exemplar 4.32 (elastic rebound on an incline): keep the incoming speed, find the angle of the rebound velocity to the horizontal, then treat it as a projection up the incline.
cards.quote: (ii) Work out angle particle speed has with horizontal after it rebounds. (iii) Rest is similar to if particle is projected up the incline.)

cards.claim: Even in an elastic collision, kinetic energy is not constant during the contact time; only the initial and final kinetic energies are equal.
cards.quote: then the initial kinetic energy is equal to the final kinetic energy but the kinetic energy during the collision time ∆t is not constant.

cards.claim: NCERT Exercise 5.14: a gas molecule hits a wall at 200 m/s at 30 degrees to the normal and rebounds with the same speed; is momentum conserved, and is the collision elastic or inelastic?
cards.quote: A molecule in a gas container hits a horizontal wall with speed 200 m s–1 and angle 30° with the normal, and rebounds with the same speed. Is momentum conserved in the collision ? Is the collision elastic or inelastic ?

question.exam: NCERT Class XI Physics Part I textbook exercises
question.paper: Chapter 5 Work, Energy and Power, Exercises (Reprint 2026-27)

cards.claim: NCERT answer to 5.14 (first part): the momentum of the molecule + wall system is conserved.
cards.quote: 5.14 Yes, momentum of the molecule + wall system is conserved.

cards.claim: NCERT answer to 5.14 (conclusion): kinetic energy is conserved, so the collision is elastic.
cards.quote: Since kinetic energy is also conserved, the collision is elastic.

The coefficient of restitution e of a collision is the ratio of the magnitudes of the final and initial relative velocities, e = vB/vA.
cards.quote: In a collision, the ratio of the magnitudes of the initial and final relative velocities is called the coefficient of restitution and denoted by the symbol e ,

cards.claim: If the final relative speed is smaller than the initial relative speed (e < 1), the kinetic energy decreases in the collision; such collisions are called inelastic.
cards.quote: If the magnitude of the final relative velocity is less than the magnitude of the initial relative velocity, e < 1, then the change in kinetic energy is negative. Collisions in which the kinetic energy decreases are called inelastic collisions,
